oriental_ortho.trinity:
Oriental Orthodox Christians confess the Holy Trinity: one God in three hypostases, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, of one essence, as the first two councils taught. The Father is the source; the Son is begotten of the Father before all ages; the Spirit proceeds from the Father. This is not three gods, nor one person wearing three masks. Worship, baptism and the Creed are Trinitarian.

The churches of this communion recite the Creed without later Western additions. Language about 'persons' and 'nature' follows the Greek and Syriac fathers, especially St Cyril. Members would recognise this as the same Nicene faith held with Eastern Orthodox and most Western Christians, even where later disputes about Christology arose.
oriental_ortho.filioque:
The Holy Spirit's procession from the Father is confessed as the Creed of 381 states it. Oriental Orthodox churches do not add 'and the Son' (the Filioque) to that article. The Father is the one source of the Godhead; the Spirit is not understood as proceeding from Father and Son as from two sources.

This is a matter of the Creed's wording and of how the Trinity is ordered, not a denial that the Son sends the Spirit in the economy of salvation. Dialogue with Catholics and Protestants often has to pause here and say that 'procession' in the Creed and 'sending' in the Gospel are not treated as the same statement.
oriental_ortho.essence_and_energies:
Oriental Orthodox speech about God distinguishes the divine nature itself from God's operations or workings toward the world, without making the Palamite vocabulary of 'essence and energies' a required school term. God is truly known in his acts of creation, incarnation, sanctification and deification, and remains beyond comprehension in his essence.

The goal of the Christian life is communion with God, not a map of inner divine distinctions. Some writers in the communion use language close to later Byzantine talk of uncreated grace; others stay with older Alexandrian and Syriac wording. The shared conviction is that grace is God himself at work, not a created substitute standing between the believer and God.
oriental_ortho.incarnation:
The Incarnation is the Son of God taking flesh from the Theotokos and becoming man for our salvation. The Word did not inhabit a man from outside; he became flesh. What is not assumed is not healed, so the full humanity of Christ is confessed together with his full divinity.

The feast of the Nativity and the hymns of St Cyril's tradition keep this as the centre of the faith. After the Incarnation there is one Lord Jesus Christ, not a pair of subjects loosely joined. How that unity is named is the subject of the communion's distinctive Christology, but the fact of the Incarnation itself is not in doubt.
oriental_ortho.natures_of_christ:
Oriental Orthodox teaching confesses one incarnate nature of God the Word: the miaphysite formula associated with St Cyril. After the union, Christ is one, without mixing, without change, without division and without separation. Divinity and humanity remain real; they are not blended into a third thing, nor split into two acting subjects.

The communion does not accept the Council of Chalcedon's 'in two natures' as the best safeguard of that faith, and rejects the label 'Monophysite' when it means Eutyches' absorption of the humanity. Modern agreed statements with Catholics and Eastern Orthodox often say the dispute was largely over words. Within the family the older Cyrillian phrase remains the native way to speak.
oriental_ortho.theosis:
Theosis, or deification, is the purpose of the Incarnation and of the sacramental life: that human beings become partakers of the divine nature by grace, not by becoming a fourth person of the Trinity. Baptism, Chrismation, the Eucharist and ascetic struggle open the person to this communion.

It is not a slogan unique to one national church. Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian teachers describe salvation as healing and glorification of the whole human being. The language can sound like Eastern Orthodox theosis; the difference, where it exists, is more in the surrounding Christological vocabulary than in the hope itself.
oriental_ortho.original_sin:
The communion speaks of ancestral sin and the fall of Adam more than of inherited guilt in the later Augustinian sense. Death, corruption and a weakened will spread to the race; infants are not treated as personally guilty of Adam's act. Baptism is still the rebirth that joins a person to Christ and frees from the dominion of death and sin.

Exact emphasis varies. Some teachers stress mortality as the main inheritance; others speak more readily of a stain or inclination. None of the churches reduces the fall to a mere bad example. Ascetic life and the mysteries presuppose that human nature needs healing, not only instruction.
oriental_ortho.canon:
Each church in the communion has a received biblical canon used in liturgy and teaching. The core of the Protestant sixty-six books is read, together with books often called deuterocanonical in the West. Ethiopian tradition is known for a wider list than the Coptic or Syriac lists; Armenian practice has its own received shape.

There is no single bound volume identical in every patriarchate. What is shared is that Scripture is read inside Holy Tradition, in the lectionary and the fathers, not as a bare text standing alone. Members would not treat 'the canon' as a closed debate settled by one Western council.
oriental_ortho.tradition:
Holy Tradition is the life of the Church handing on the apostolic faith: Scripture, liturgy, councils the communion receives, the fathers, the canons and the living practice of the monasteries and parishes. It is not a second book beside the Bible, nor a license to invent. Scripture is the heart of Tradition and is heard within it.

When Oriental Orthodox say a teaching is traditional, they mean it has been prayed and guarded in the churches of Alexandria, Antioch, Armenia, Ethiopia and India, not that a modern committee voted it in. Disputes with other Christians about the pope or about Chalcedon are argued as disputes about which stream truly kept that Tradition.
oriental_ortho.papal_primacy:
Oriental Orthodox churches honour the ancient sees and can speak of a primacy of honour among bishops, but they do not accept papal primacy as universal ordinary jurisdiction or as a condition of being the Church. Each catholicos or pope (the Coptic pope of Alexandria is a patriarch, not the bishop of Rome) heads his church in council with his synod.

Rome is treated as a sister see with a real historic prestige, not as the court of final appeal. Agreements and tensions with the Catholic Church in recent decades have not changed the working rule: communion is synodal and autocephalous within this family.
oriental_ortho.ecumenical_councils:
The communion receives three ecumenical councils as the dogmatic foundation: Nicaea in 325, Constantinople in 381 and Ephesus in 431. Those councils confess the Trinity, the full divinity of the Son and of the Spirit, and that Mary is Theotokos against Nestorius.

Chalcedon in 451 and the later councils recognised by Eastern Orthodox and Catholics are not received as ecumenical here. Local synods and later fathers still matter for law and piety. When members say 'the councils,' they usually mean those first three unless they are explaining a conversation with Chalcedonian Christians.
oriental_ortho.apostolic_succession:
Bishops stand in apostolic succession by ordination in the historic line of the sees of Alexandria, Antioch, Armenia, Ethiopia and the Malankara church. Succession is not only a chain of hands; it is succession in the apostolic faith and in the eucharistic assembly.

Ordination is performed by bishops of the communion, with the liturgy and the laying on of hands. Claims of succession detached from that faith, or claims that succession failed in these churches after Chalcedon, are rejected. The churches regard themselves as the continuation of the ancient patriarchates of those regions.
oriental_ortho.confirmation:
Chrismation is the sealing with holy myron immediately after Baptism, conferring the gift of the Holy Spirit. In these churches it is not delayed until adolescence as a separate Western confirmation class. The newly baptised, including infants, are chrismated and commonly receive the Eucharist.

The myron is consecrated by the patriarch or catholicos. The rite belongs with Baptism as one initiation. Calling it 'confirmation' can mislead a Western reader into thinking of a later maturity rite; the native name and the native order are Chrismation at the font.
oriental_ortho.liturgy:
The Divine Liturgy, also called Holy Qurbana in the Syriac and Indian churches, is the centre of parish life: the offering of the Body and Blood of Christ. Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian and Malankara rites differ in language, chant and ceremonial, but all are sacrificial, eucharistic and reserved to the ordained priesthood.

The faithful prepare by fasting and confession according to local custom. The liturgy is not a teaching meeting with communion attached; it is the mystery in which the Church becomes what she is. Visitors from Western Protestant services will find the length, the incense and the standing prayer unfamiliar, but members experience it as the ordinary Sunday.
oriental_ortho.icons:
Icons are holy images of Christ, the Theotokos and the saints, used in church and home as part of prayer, not as decorations only. They are honoured, not worshipped as gods. Ethiopian manuscript painting, Coptic iconography and Armenian khachkars belong to the same conviction that the Incarnation makes matter capable of bearing witness to the persons depicted.

Practice is not identical in every parish. Some traditions paint more freely; some older Syriac settings are more reserved. The shared rule is that honour given to the image passes to the prototype, and that rejecting all images as idols misunderstands what the churches are doing.
oriental_ortho.fasting:
Fasting is a regular, demanding part of church life: abstinence from animal foods and often from dairy on many days of the year, especially Great Lent, the fasts before major feasts and the weekly Wednesday and Friday rhythm. Ethiopian and Eritrean practice is among the strictest in Christianity; Coptic, Syriac and Armenian calendars are also substantial.

Fasting is not a private diet. It is tied to liturgy, almsgiving and confession. Economia, pastoral relaxation for the sick, travellers and the poor, is recognised. Members would not treat fasting as optional decoration on an otherwise Protestant year.
oriental_ortho.sign_of_the_cross:
The sign of the cross is made constantly: entering church, beginning prayer, passing an icon, receiving a blessing. Oriental Orthodox practice commonly uses two or three fingers according to local custom, touching forehead, chest and shoulders. It is a confession of the Trinity and of the Cross, not a superstition bolted onto worship.

Clergy bless with the sign; the faithful sign themselves. A visitor who never sees the gesture is not in an ordinary parish of this communion. Exact finger position can mark regional habit more than dogma.
oriental_ortho.jesus_prayer:
The Jesus Prayer — 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me' — is used in monastic and lay devotion, especially where the hesychast and desert traditions have been received. It is not the only form of prayer; the liturgies, psalms and intercessions remain first.

Use is uneven. Some Coptic and Ethiopian monastics know it as a way of unceasing prayer; some parishioners know only the liturgical responses. It should not be described as a required technique. Where it is taught, it is repentance in a short sentence, not a method for producing visions.
oriental_ortho.mary:
Mary is honoured as Theotokos, Mother of God, ever-virgin, the highest of the saints. Churches and fasts are dedicated to her. She is not a fourth person of the Trinity and not a co-redeemer in later Western slogans; she is the one from whom the Word took flesh, and therefore she is named in every liturgy.

Hymns call her more honourable than the cherubim. Asking her prayers is ordinary. Protestant nervousness that this crowds out Christ is answered, in this tradition, by pointing to the Incarnation: honour to the Mother is honour to the Son who made her his temple.
oriental_ortho.theotokos:
The title Theotokos, God-bearer or Mother of God, is a Christological confession from Ephesus: the one born of Mary is the Word, so she is Mother of God, not mother of a man later joined to God. Oriental Orthodox churches treat this as settled dogma.

Christotokos alone is heard as the Nestorian dodge the third council rejected. Piety follows the title: icons of the Mother and Child, the hymnody of the liturgy, and the insistence that the child in her arms is one Lord, not two sons.
oriental_ortho.assumption:
The Dormition is the falling asleep of the Theotokos and her being taken by her Son. The feast is kept with fasting beforehand in several of the churches. The tradition holds that she died a real death and that her body was not left to corruption, though scholastic definitions like the later Catholic dogma of the Assumption are not the native framing.

Armenian, Coptic, Syriac and Ethiopian calendars all keep the feast. Members would speak of the Mother of God being translated to life, not of a detailed map of the event. The point is her share in her Son's victory over death.
oriental_ortho.intercession_of_saints:
The intercession of the saints is asked in every liturgy: the Theotokos, the apostles, the local martyrs and the monastic fathers. The saints are alive in Christ and pray; the Church on earth asks them to pray. This is not thought of as replacing the unique mediation of Christ, but as the family of the redeemed speaking to one another.

Relics and icons belong with this practice. A member would find a service that never names the saints strangely bare. The distinction between worship due to God and honour due to the saints is taught, even when popular devotion is warm.
oriental_ortho.prayers_for_the_dead:
Prayers for the departed are part of the liturgy, memorial Saturdays and funeral rites. The Church commends the dead to the mercy of God and does not treat death as the end of belonging to the eucharistic body. This is not the same system as Latin purgatory with its tariff of satisfactions.

Coptic and Ethiopian funeral and memorial customs are especially full. Members pray for the repose of the soul and trust God's judgment. Speculation about exact intermediate geography is less central than keeping the names of the dead in the prayer of the Church.
